title: Two Thousand Feet
passage:
A contrail that lasts is mostly not the airplane’s doing. The engine puts out heat, water vapor and a great many specks of soot, and if the air the plume mixes into is cold enough, the mixture passes briefly through the point at which liquid water condenses; droplets form on the specks and freeze almost at once. That much is over in seconds. Everything after it belongs to the air the airplane happened to be crossing. Usually that air is dry with respect to ice, the crystals hand their water back, and the line behind the wing is gone inside a minute or two. Sometimes it is not dry. In a layer already carrying more vapor than ice can hold at that temperature, the crystals do not shrink but feed, and go on feeding, so that by the time a contrail is an hour old most of the ice in it was never inside an engine. It came out of the air the airplane was passing through.

The awkward part is that a layer like that has nothing in it to look at. Air can sit well past ice saturation and make no cloud of its own, because starting a crystal from nothing needs roughly half again as much vapor as keeping an existing one alive. So the sky stays clear, the layer runs a couple of hundred miles with a depth that would fit inside a small hill, and the first anyone knows of it is the mark an airplane leaves crossing it. The forecasts are not much help either. Temperature at altitude is predicted well. Humidity at altitude is predicted from almost nothing, because almost nothing up there measures it, and the models were built for weather that reaches the ground.

Two winters ago a control center began moving airplanes anyway. On nights when the forecast laid one of these layers across a route, the flight was planned two thousand feet beneath it, and the crews were told why. Nights only: a spreading contrail holds in heat that would otherwise leave, and in daylight it also turns some sunlight back toward space, so the two effects pull against one another, while after dark there is nothing pulling the other way. Sunniva Vestrigg, who built the forecast the center used, is unsentimental about what it can do. “The layers are usually shallow enough that one step down is out of them,” she says. “Which night, and which fifty miles of the route – that is what we get wrong.”

Anselm Colverdine audits what the airplanes actually did, and his numbers are the least comfortable part of the record. Of 141 flights that were left alone and flew straight through a forecast layer, 61 left a mark anybody could find afterward. The forecast was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it. Of 406 plans written with the step-down in them, 96 were flown that way; the rest were traded away for traffic, for weather, for a crew that wanted the fuel. An adjusted airplane burned about two percent more than it would have. Spread over everything the sector handled that winter, the extra came to a fraction of a percent. “The maneuver is the cheap part,” Colverdine says. “It was always going to be the cheap part.”

Which leaves the counting. A contrail cannot be seen at the moment it is made; it needs anywhere from five minutes to an hour to spread wide enough for a satellite to register it, and by then the wind has carried it well away from where it was born. The picture is flat, so nothing in it says how high the thing is. On a busy evening four or five tracks cross the same square of sky. And a success looks like an empty picture. So does a forecast that was wrong, and a contrail too thin to register, and a sheet of cloud sitting over the top of one. A picture that shows a contrail settles that one flight. An empty one settles nothing, and only one of the readings it allows blames the forecast; two are the camera’s, and the fourth is the success the flight was after. That the forecast asks for more than the sky supplies is the best of those readings, and the forecast’s own author reads it the same way, but it is a reading of the empty frames and not a count taken from them. Vestrigg wants humidity sensors flying on the airliners themselves, a hundred of them to begin with, and believes the rest would follow. Perhaps it would. But the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced. Colverdine is right about the cheap part, and the findings that will outlast the trial are his: that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for, and that most of the descents it asks for are never flown. The second of those comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all. A third winter is being flown. The sensors have not been fitted.
– Lorcan Trawsfield

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: How hard it is to predict humidity at the heights where airliners cruise.
A cheap change of altitude, and the trouble of showing that it worked.
How the ice crystals behind an airplane grow when the surrounding air is already wet.
How much of aviation’s warming comes from cloud rather than from burning fuel.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text focus), edge position 1. WHY-KEY (B): the passage is built from one asymmetry that every paragraph feeds. Moving an airplane is trivial: two thousand feet, written into the flight plan, about two percent more fuel on the flight that takes it and a fraction of a percent across the sector. Knowing whether it did anything is not: the layer is invisible before the crossing, the humidity forecast is made from almost no measurements, and afterward a satellite that cannot see a young contrail, cannot see its height, and cannot tell four or five tracks apart is asked to certify an absence. Colverdine says the maneuver was always going to be the cheap part, and the writer’s own closing sentences say the same. B names both halves and claims nothing more. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error – the humidity forecast is one strand of paragraph 2, and it is the reason for one of the two findings the writer rates, but it explains nothing about paragraph 1, nothing about the plans that were never flown, and nothing about the satellite’s three separate blindnesses in paragraph 5; it is the option for a reader who takes the most technical-sounding difficulty in a piece for its subject. C = surface_word_match over a part-for-whole scope error – it recycles the passage’s most distinctive vocabulary (crystals, ice, wet air), and unlike A it names something the text really does give room to: crystal growth is the back half of paragraph 1, from “Usually that air is dry with respect to ice” through the punchline that most of the ice in an hour-old contrail was never inside an engine. What makes C wrong is proportion, not accuracy. Paragraph 1 is the premise the piece argues from – the air, and not the airplane, decides whether a mark lasts – and paragraphs 3 to 5, the trial, the audit and the counting, do not touch crystal growth at all; paragraph 2 comes back to crystals only to explain why a layer that would feed them carries no cloud of its own, which is a different mechanism (starting one needs about half again the vapor that feeding one does) and a different point. D = outside_knowledge – a real and much-repeated claim about aviation and cloud. The passage does say that a contrail holds in heat, because the night-only rule turns on it; what is absent is the comparison. The text never sets that heat against the heat from burning the fuel, never quantifies either, and mentions fuel only as the thing a crew wanted more of and an adjusted airplane burned two percent more of.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the layers themselves?

options.text: They are shallow, and they hold no cloud.
They form where thin cirrus is already present.
They can be picked out from the flight deck.
They spread outward once an airplane has crossed them.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), local order, anchored in paragraph 2; this is the unit’s short-breath item (eight-word stem, options of eight or nine words). WHY-KEY (A): paragraph 2 gives exactly two properties. The layer has “nothing in it to look at” and makes “no cloud of its own”, because starting a crystal from nothing needs roughly half again as much vapor as keeping one alive; and it runs a couple of hundred miles across with “a depth that would fit inside a small hill”, which is why two thousand feet is enough to leave it. A paraphrases both and stops. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = reversal of the paragraph’s central point, and the most tempting option for a reader who knows that contrails and cirrus are the same substance; the passage says the opposite, that the air stays clear precisely because it is short of what a new crystal needs. C = outside_knowledge dressed as plausibility – crews do see weather, but the passage’s whole reason for calling the layer awkward is that “the first anyone knows of it is the mark an airplane leaves crossing it”. D = surface_word_match with the wrong subject: it is the contrail that spreads, over five minutes to an hour, not the layer; the option lifts the verb from paragraph 5 and attaches it to the noun from paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the decision to move night flights only?

options.text: Traffic after dark was light enough for the center to move the airplanes freely.
The forecast layers found at night were deeper than those found by day.
A contrail made in daylight cools the ground instead of warming it.
After dark nothing works against the warming, since no sunlight is turned away.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), local order, anchored in paragraph 3; the step is short but it is a step, which is why the item is not filed as retrieval. WHY-KEY (D): the passage gives one reason for the night-only rule and only one, and it gives it in two halves. A spreading contrail “holds in heat that would otherwise leave”; in daylight “it also turns some sunlight back toward space, so the two effects pull against one another, while after dark there is nothing pulling the other way.” D joins the halves. What pulls the other way is the sunlight, night is what removes the sunlight, so after dark nothing is left working against the heat the contrail is holding in. The reader supplies the join and re-describes the held-in heat as the warming; nothing else is added, and the passage supports no second joining. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = plausible operational reason the passage never gives, and the option a cautious reader reaches for because it sounds like the sober, practical answer; the text’s only remark about how busy the sky is comes later and cuts the other way, since on a busy evening four or five tracks cross the same square. This is the unit’s law-10 break: the flat assertion is keyed and the careful-sounding option is wrong. B = invented comparison, built from real nouns in the paragraph (forecast, layers, night) but stating a night-versus-day difference in depth that the passage never mentions; the only depth given is the small hill, and it is not time-of-day dependent. C = quantifier_upgrade – the passage names both effects and then stops. “Also” adds the sunlight effect to the heat-holding rather than replacing it, and “pull against one another” says that the two oppose, not which of them wins; no sentence anywhere in the text delivers a net verdict for daylight, and the word cool is never used of a contrail. C supplies the verdict, and supplies it in the direction readers most often overshoot. What defeats it is not that the passage settles the daylight sum the other way – the passage does not settle it at all – but that a stem asking what we are told cannot be answered with a thing the text conspicuously leaves open.

questions.prompt: What is implied by the flights that were left alone?

options.text: Fewer than half of them were flying where the forecast had put a layer.
The forecast was missing most of the wet layers that were really there.
Many of the descents that were flown will have bought nothing.
They were cruising at heights where a contrail could not form at all.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. WHY-KEY (C): 141 airplanes were sent through air the forecast had called wet, nothing was done to them, and 61 left a mark. The writer reads Colverdine’s number in the next sentence – the forecast “was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it” – and closes the loop in paragraph 5, where he names among the findings that will outlast the trial “that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for”. The step the reader has to take is the one the passage stops just short of: the descents that were flown were planned on that same over-calling forecast, so a large share of them were made into air that would have produced nothing anyway. One inch, and the passage supports no second one. Paragraph 5 hedges its own reading of the empty frames – a forecast asking for more than the sky supplies is the best of those readings, not a count taken from them – and C is pitched at exactly that strength: many of the descents rather than all of them, and will have bought nothing rather than bought nothing. The inference inherits the hedge instead of stepping past it. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = mangled quantity, the trap for a reader who carries “fewer than half” across to the wrong noun. Fewer than half of the 141 left a mark; ALL of them were flying where the forecast had put a layer, which is the whole design of the comparison and is stated in the same sentence. B = the reversal, and the sharpest distractor here: a false negative offered where the passage documents a false positive. Nothing in the trial could have found a layer the forecast failed to call, because only called layers were flown through on purpose. C requires reading the arrow the right way around. D = outside_knowledge plus a two-step leap – cruising altitude does govern whether a contrail forms at all, which is why the option sounds informed, but 61 of these flights left marks, which settles it on the page.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude toward the satellite count?

options.text: He thinks it settled less than the center’s own records did.
He expects sensors on the airliners to settle what the pictures cannot.
He gives both kinds of evidence their due and prefers neither.
He regards the imagery as worthless and would put an end to it.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / tone / attitude), whole-text item, signature trap role_or_attribution_swap. WHY-KEY (A): the writer’s own voice arrives in the last third of paragraph 5 and takes a side without hedging. He calls the satellite count “the smallest thing those two winters produced”, says flatly that “Colverdine is right about the cheap part”, and then names what he does rate: “the findings that will outlast the trial are his” – that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for, and that most of the descents it asks for are never flown – adding that the second of them comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all. Ranking the imagery below the paperwork is the position the paragraph is written to reach, and the paragraph is careful about how far the ranking goes: the first of the two findings is granted as the best reading the empty frames will carry, not as something the pictures counted. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = role_or_attribution_swap, the family’s signature and the trap for a reader who takes the last confident technical voice for the writer’s: wanting a hundred instrumented airliners is Vestrigg’s hope, given in her name, and the writer answers it with a three-word shrug and an immediate “But”. C = tone_misread, and the option that sounds like what a reporter ought to do; “the smallest thing those two winters produced”, followed immediately by “Colverdine is right”, is precisely what a writer preferring neither would not write. This is the second law-10 break in the unit: the judicious-sounding option is wrong and the flat one is keyed. D = polarity overshoot – he explains at length why an empty picture cannot certify anything, but in the same breath he grants that “a picture that shows a contrail settles that one flight”, he never asks for the counting to stop, and he lets Vestrigg’s wish stand as a possibility rather than an error. Worthless is a word for evidence that says nothing either way; his complaint is narrower than that and is about absences.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: Every physical claim in this passage was checked against the primary literature BEFORE the passage was written, because batch15's ELF unit was refuted at V-FINAL for stating a mechanism backwards. Verified 2026-08-26. The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any query, so all verification ran through Exa web search (MCP) and, for name checks, Exa plus exact-phrase fetches of Mojeek and Brave result pages; every query below is re-runnable. (1) FORMATION: a contrail forms when hot, moist exhaust mixes with cold ambient air and the mixture transiently reaches saturation with respect to LIQUID water, at which point droplets condense on emitted soot particles and freeze almost instantly - Schmidt-Appleman criterion. Sources: ACP 24/9219 (2024) 'Understanding the role of contrails and contrail cirrus in climate change'; ACP 26/10695 (2026); ACP 21/16817 (2021). The passage's sentence 'the mixture passes briefly through the point at which liquid water condenses; droplets form on the specks and freeze almost at once' is this criterion and not the ice condition, which is deliberate. (2) PERSISTENCE is a SEPARATE condition and requires the AMBIENT air to be supersaturated with respect to ICE; formation can occur where the ambient air is subsaturated with respect to ice, and in that case the crystals sublimate within minutes. Sources: ACP 26/10695 explicitly ('contrail formation requires plume saturation with respect to liquid water, which can occur even when the ambient atmosphere is subsaturated with respect to ice. However, for contrails to become persistent ... ambient ice supersaturation is additionally required'); acp-24-7911-2024 (Gierens/Hofer, 'How well can persistent contrails be predicted? An update'). Getting these two round the wrong way is the exact failure mode this note exists to prevent. (3) MOST CONTRAILS ARE SHORT-LIVED because most upper-tropospheric air is not ice-supersaturated: Megill and Grewe, ACP 25/4131 (2025), find 92.3 % of grid cells are not ice-supersaturated and name persistence the binding constraint. The passage's 'Usually that air is dry with respect to ice ... gone inside a minute or two' matches. (4) MOST OF THE ICE IS AMBIENT, NOT ENGINE WATER: Voigt et al., Communications Earth and Environment 2 (2021), measured a one-minute-old contrail ice water content of 4.98 kg per kg fuel of which 'only about a quarter ... was emitted by the engines, the remainder had condensed from the supersaturated ambient atmosphere'. The passage's 'most of the ice in it was never inside an engine' is this, stated for an older contrail where the ambient share is larger still. (5) THE LAYER IS INVISIBLE: ice-supersaturated air routinely carries no cloud, because nucleating a new crystal needs far higher humidity than sustaining an existing one - homogeneous freezing onset is measured at 152 %, 155 % and 162 % RHi at -42.5, -47.5 and -52.5 C (DeMott et al., PNAS/PMC299754), with heterogeneous thresholds around 120-130 % (Haag et al., ACP 3/1791, 2003; Krämer et al. as used in the DLR mid-latitude lidar study). Jensen et al. and Baumgardner (2000JD900526) report ice supersaturation on 5-20 % of flight segments where NO ice crystals were detected; the DLR lidar study finds 6.8 % of cloud-free points supersaturated. The passage's 'roughly half again as much vapor as keeping an existing one alive' is the ~150 % homogeneous figure, hedged with 'roughly'. (6) GEOMETRY: ice-supersaturated regions are 'tens to hundreds of kilometers long horizontally, but only a few hundred meters thin vertically', which is precisely why an altitude change of order 2000 ft is the operational lever - NASA TM-20250007272, 'Review of Past Decade of Aviation Contrail Research'. The passage's 'a couple of hundred miles ... a depth that would fit inside a small hill' and its two-thousand-foot step-down are both inside this. (7) FORECAST ASYMMETRY: temperature at cruise level is predicted well, so the formation criterion is predicted well; ice supersaturation is not, and Gierens et al. (2020) describe forecasting it at a given time and place as 'currently almost like tossing a coin' (ETS 0.08 raw, 0.378 for the best regression in acp-24-7911-2024). Named causes: strong variability in the water vapor field, very few humidity measurements at cruise level for assimilation, and crude ice-cloud parameterisations, because ice supersaturation 'hardly affects the weather on the ground'. The passage's 'Temperature at altitude is predicted well. Humidity at altitude is predicted from almost nothing ... the models were built for weather that reaches the ground' is a paraphrase of that passage of the literature. (8) DIURNAL SIGN: contrail radiative forcing is dominated by longwave warming; in daylight the shortwave albedo effect partially cancels it, and at night there is no cancellation. Stuber and Forster, ACP 7/3153 (2007): night flights are under 40 % of global distance flown but contribute about 60 % of the annual mean forcing, and during daytime about 62 % of the longwave effect is offset by the shortwave effect. Note the sign: daytime contrails are on average LESS warming, not cooling, which is why Q3's option C is a distractor and not a second key. Teoh et al., ACP 24/6071 (2024), confirm the same asymmetry and add that contrails formed 03:00-12:00 LT are the ones most likely to end up net cooling. (9) CONCENTRATION (background only, not asserted in the passage): about 2.7 % of flights caused 80 % of global contrail energy forcing in 2019, 12 % in the North Atlantic, 2.2 % over Japan - ACP 24/6071; ACP 22/10919; Teoh 2020 thesis. (10) COST: real trials measure about a 2 % fuel increase per adjusted flight (Sonabend et al., Communications Engineering, 2024) against a fleet-wide penalty estimated at 0.1-0.2 % (Teoh et al. 2020; Frias et al. 2024; Dean et al. 2025). The passage's 'about two percent more' on the adjusted airplane and 'a fraction of a percent' across the sector are these two numbers and are consistent with each other. (11) FORECAST FALSE POSITIVES: in the 2024 randomized trial, of 22 control flights deliberately flown through forecast contrail-formation zones only 11 produced an observed contrail, a hit rate the authors call high relative to earlier work. The passage's invented 61-of-141 is the same phenomenon at a lower rate and is presented as invented data, not as that trial. (12) VERIFICATION: contrails are not observable at the moment of formation; the time to become detectable in GOES-16 imagery ranges from about 5 minutes to 1 hour, during which the contrail advects away from where it formed; the satellite view is two-dimensional so carries no altitude; dense traffic causes contrail-to-flight misattribution; and roughly 42-45 % of contrail distance is observable in a given frame. Sources: AMT 18/3495 (2025), 'Benchmarking and improving algorithms for attributing satellite-observed contrails to flights'; Communications Engineering 2024 methods and limitations. Every clause of paragraph 5's list is one of these. (13) TAKE RATE: in a 2026 airline-led randomized trial, 1232 flights were marked eligible and contrail-optimized plans were released, but only 112 were flown as planned, the authors naming take rate 'a primary bottleneck'. The passage's invented 96 of 406 is this phenomenon. (14) INSTRUMENTED AIRLINERS as the proposed fix: the humidity data the forecasting literature repeatedly asks for comes from instrumented passenger aircraft (MOZAIC/IAGOS), which is what Vestrigg's 'humidity sensors flying on the airliners themselves' names. Nothing in the passage asserts anything outside this verified set; all people, counts, dates, quotations, the control center, the sector and the third winter are invented on top of it. ADDENDUM 2026-08-26 (round-2 repair; nothing above this sentence is rewritten). The repair added one clause to paragraph 3 and three sentences to paragraph 5, and both are inside the set already verified here. Paragraph 3's new 'holds in heat that would otherwise leave' is item (8)'s first half stated without the word warming: contrail radiative forcing is dominated by longwave trapping, the daylight shortwave term partially offsets it (about 62 % of the longwave effect offset in daytime, Stuber and Forster 2007), and the passage still declines to state a net daylight sign, which is what keeps Teoh et al. 2024's 03:00-12:00 LT cooling result outside the text rather than contradicted by it. Paragraph 5's new sentences assert only that a frame showing a contrail is informative about that flight and that an empty frame is not, which is item (12): about 42-45 % of contrail distance is observable in a given frame, detection lags formation by 5 minutes to 1 hour, the view carries no altitude, and dense traffic causes misattribution - every one of these can hide a contrail and none can manufacture one, so the detection floor is a floor and the absence is not a count. That asymmetry is the reason the repaired paragraph books the forecast's over-calling as the best reading of the empty frames rather than as a measurement, and books only the take rate (item 13) to the center's own paperwork.

But'; Q5/C by 'the smallest thing those two winters produced' plus 'Colverdine is right'; Q5/D by the absence of any call to stop counting and by the third winter now being flown. FOUR ITEMS WERE REWRITTEN DURING THIS PASS, two of them on the second, adversarial reading. edits.note: MAJOR fix, part 1. Three sentences inserted at the point where the reader is still holding the four-causes list, which is where the epistemics belong. They state the asymmetry the detection literature actually supports (mechanism_verification_note item 12: roughly 42-45 % of contrail distance is observable in a frame, detection lags formation by 5 minutes to 1 hour, the view carries no altitude, dense traffic causes misattribution): every one of those limits can hide a contrail and none can manufacture one, so a positive frame is informative about that flight and an empty frame is not. The over-calling is therefore booked as the best reading the empty frames will carry - corroborated from outside the imagery by the forecast's own author, who says in paragraph 3 which night and which fifty miles is what they get wrong - and explicitly not as a count. That is the strongest claim the evidence licenses, and it is the claim the passage now makes. +76 mech tokens.
